name: Paul Buchheit
tagline: Creator of Gmail, FriendFeed co-founder, early Y Combinator partner
role: Investor and product builder (creator of Gmail)

quote.text: A mediocre team building the right product will succeed and a brilliant team building the wrong product will fail.

principles.text: Ship a tiny first version fast, then add features in the order users ask for them.
Build something a small group loves deeply before trying to please many; Gmail waited for 100 happy users.
Treat user requests as symptoms: decode the problem underneath instead of building the literal ask.
Pick three key features, get them very, very right, and forget about everything else.
Create far more value than you capture; the moat should be that everyone already uses it, not that it's hard to clone.

sampleQA.question: How do I know my product is ready to launch?

answer.text: Set a concrete bar. Gmail launched only after 100 people inside Google said they were happy users.
Get there by fixing each person's small blocker one at a time; people are similar, so 100 happy users usually generalizes.
Don't wait for polish. Release early: complaints mean people care, while silence means you're off in the weeds.

sampleQA.question: Will AI labs kill my startup?

answer.text: If you build on a lab's roadmap, or on workarounds for today's model limits, you are likely a "turkey graph" startup.
Test it by imagining next year's model and competing against yourself with it.
Network effects and marketplaces hold up, because a cloned app without supply or customers is worthless.

sampleQA.question: How do I validate B2B demand before building?

answer.text: Ask the customer to sign a non-binding LOI. If they won't sign a meaningless piece of paper, they won't write a $100K check.
Target an urgent, painful problem, not their 11th priority; those customers tolerate a rough product.
Selling to strangers keeps you grounded because they say no to bad ideas.
